opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic case is pretty simple. A lot of AGI safety work is about trying to make the model itself not want to do bad things: alignment, interpretability, better training signals, that sort of thing. I think that's really important, and it's a big part of what our team does. But we should be honest that we might not fully succeed at it, at least not on the timelines we're likely to face. So you want a second line of defense: even if the model *were* misaligned and trying to do something bad, could we stop it from actually causing harm? That's roughly what we mean by AI control.

Once you frame it that way, a lot of control starts to look like security. The threat model is something like an insider threat. You have a very capable agent with legitimate access to your infrastructure, your code, maybe its own weights, and you want to make sure that if it tried to, say, exfiltrate itself or sabotage research, you'd catch it or it simply wouldn't be able to. Security teams have been thinking about insider threats, least privilege, monitoring, access control and auditing for decades. So a lot of the hard-won knowledge you need already lives there.

Why do I think these roles in particular are impactful? A few reasons.

First, the bottleneck has shifted. A couple of years ago, control was mostly a research question: what protocols even make sense, how do you evaluate them, how do you red-team them? There's still lots of research to do. But increasingly the question is, can we actually implement this in the real systems where models are deployed internally, with real codebases, real permissions and real engineering constraints? That's an engineering problem, and it's one where a small number of competent people can make a big difference.

Second, you're working where the risk actually is. The scenarios I worry about most involve models being used heavily inside the lab, doing a lot of coding and research autonomously. Those internal deployments are exactly where the security team has leverage. If you're building the monitoring, sandboxing and permission systems for those agents, you're directly shaping whether a misaligned model could cause a catastrophe.

Third, it's a relatively neglected skill set within safety. The safety community has a lot of people with ML research backgrounds, and comparatively few people who are both serious security engineers and take misalignment risk seriously. If you have that combination, your counterfactual impact is pretty large.

And finally, there's a nice robustness property: much of this work is valuable regardless of how optimistic or pessimistic you are about alignment. Good security and monitoring around powerful AI systems helps against misuse, against external attackers, and against misaligned models. It's hard to regret having built it.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI control as a second line of defense against harm from misaligned models, but it does not say that control will underpin Google DeepMind’s argument about Gemini or address loss of control in the medium term.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic case is pretty simple. If you buy that we might end up with AI systems that are highly capable but that we can't fully trust — maybe because alignment turned out to be harder than we hoped, maybe because we just can't verify alignment well enough by the time we're deploying them — then you want a second line of defence. That's what control is: it's the set of techniques that let you get useful work out of a model even under the assumption that it might be trying to undermine you. Monitoring its actions, restricting what it can do, having untrusted models checked by trusted ones, auditing suspicious behaviour, that kind of thing.

What I like about it is that it doesn't depend on solving the deep conceptual problems. You don't need to know what the model "really wants." You just need to make it very hard for a misaligned model to actually cause a catastrophe without getting caught. And that's an engineering problem in a way that a lot of alignment research isn't yet. You can measure it. You can red-team it. You can ask, "If I were a scheming model with this level of access, what could I do?" and then go close that off.

The reason the security team specifically matters is that a lot of this lives at the intersection of ML and classical security. If you're worried about a model exfiltrating its own weights, or inserting backdoors into the code it writes for you, or escalating its permissions inside your infrastructure — those are security questions as much as they're AI questions. The security people already think adversarially by default. They already have the instinct of "assume the thing inside your perimeter is hostile." So pairing that mindset with people who understand how these models behave is, I think, where you get the strongest version of control.

And there's a practical point too. This is work that has to happen inside a frontier lab, because the models and the infrastructure are there. You can write papers about control from the outside, and that's valuable, but somebody has to actually build the monitoring systems, run them on real deployments, hit the real failure modes, and iterate. That's not glamorous research. A lot of it is building pipelines and figuring out why the monitor false-positives on 5% of actions. But if things go badly with alignment, that infrastructure is what stands between a misaligned model and it actually doing damage.

So when I say it's particularly impactful, I mean: the people who do this well will have shaped whether we can safely deploy models we don't fully trust, which is quite plausibly the situation we'll actually be in. And right now there just aren't that many people with the combination of skills to do it. If you're a strong engineer who cares about this stuff, the marginal value of you showing up is really high.

r001.rationale: The response says control could help safely deploy models that are not fully trusted and could prevent a misaligned model from causing damage. It does not state that control will underpin Google DeepMind’s argument about Gemini, or address harm from loss of control in the medium term.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic case is that, if we’re going to build very capable AI systems, we want safeguards that still work even when the model itself is behaving in ways we didn’t intend. You don’t want your entire safety case to depend on having successfully aligned the model.

AI control is about that additional layer: can we limit what a model has access to, monitor its actions, and prevent it from causing serious harm even if it’s trying to circumvent our safeguards? That makes security engineering a pretty natural place for this work. You’re thinking about an adversary, the permissions it has, and the ways it might get around your defenses.

The particular attraction of doing that at a frontier lab is the connection to actual systems. You can turn a proposed safeguard into something that’s implemented, test whether it works, and find out where the assumptions break down. And if it does work, you’re in a position to have it protect the systems where those risks could arise.

So I wouldn’t say control solves the whole alignment problem. But it could be an important, complementary line of defense, and engineering is what makes that defense real.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI control as a complementary safeguard against harm, but does not say it will probably underpin Google DeepMind’s argument that Gemini will not cause harm through loss of control in the medium term.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic reason is that these roles are about making sure we can remain safe even if our AI systems aren’t trying to do what we want. A lot of alignment work asks, “How do we get the model to have the right motivations?” Control asks, “Suppose we failed at that. Can we still prevent it from causing a catastrophe?” I think having that second line of defence is really valuable.

For example, imagine using an AI system to write code. You might want to ensure that it can’t insert a vulnerability that escapes review, access sensitive information it doesn’t need, or send that information somewhere else. That involves a combination of security engineering, monitoring, restricting permissions, and testing whether a sufficiently capable model could get around those measures.

And being at Google DeepMind means you can work on those problems close to the systems you’re trying to secure. You can test your assumptions against actual models and help build safeguards into the infrastructure where they’ll be used. That connection between the research question and the deployed system is a big part of the appeal.

I wouldn’t say control solves the whole alignment problem. Its effectiveness depends on what the models can do and what opportunities they have. But it gives us another way to reduce risk, and a lot of the work requires strong engineering skills. So it’s a concrete way for engineers to contribute directly to AGI safety.

r001.rationale: The response describes control as a valuable second line of defence, but does not say it will probably underpin Google DeepMind’s argument that Gemini will not cause harm through loss of control in the medium term.
